paragraphs: This plastic apple pie toy from 1989 shrinks a boxed fast food dessert into a palm-sized keepsake for retro shelves and collector scenes. Its 4,256 polygons and 4,320 vertices go into the rounded carton corners, the crimped pastry lip and the soft molded seams. At 9.22 x 2.91 x H4.28 cm, the piece fits comfortably in a child's hand or beside a lunchbox.

StemCell certification means the toy loads with matching materials in the major 3D packages, so a scene can move between tools safely. The UVs overlap, which lets repeated red plastic faces share one texture region and keeps the map count small.

Two versions are offered at $13 each: the main McDonalds apple pie toy and a Vintage Toy Apple Pie in Box Plastic Red. The red box version keeps the same polygon count, so the choice comes down to branding rather than mesh density. The plain variant is Royalty Free, while the branded version is limited to Editorial Uses Only, which fits nostalgia features and collector guides. Available since 2025, the pair suits eighties bedroom sets, attic finds and museum cases.

A whole kiwi with real fur on its brown skin, light enough to fill fruit bowls, market crates and breakfast tables. The oval body takes only 1,336 polygons and 670 vertices, so the fuzzy look comes from fur strands rather than dense geometry. Its slightly flattened sides and the small dry tip at one end match how the fruit actually rests on a counter.

CheckMate Pro certification guarantees clean topology, sensible naming and a model that opens without repair work. Non-overlapping UVs let a skin texture wrap evenly around the egg shape before the hair layer grows on top. Because the mesh is so light, many instances can stay in one scene while the viewport remains responsive.

Two versions share the page at $12 each: the Kiwi Fruit with Fur and the Tropical Fruit Kiwi with Fur. The tropical version carries 1,368 polygons, about 2% more, which gives its outline a slightly different curve. Available since 2023, the fruit suits grocery visuals, smoothie recipes and healthy eating explainers.

Corrugated cardboard folds into a rounded sci-fi capsule here, giving a pet corner in a modern apartment an unexpected centerpiece. Most of the 34,268 polygons trace the curved panels and their layered edges, while 17,250 vertices keep the shell manageable. The entry hole sits low at the front, so a cat can be posed peeking out or curled inside.

StemCell certification means materials render consistently across the main DCC packages after a file moves between applications. Non-overlapping UVs make it simple to replace the plain cardboard print with a pattern, a solid color or a worn texture.

Two products appear on the page at $5 each: the Futuristic Cardboard Cat Bed and a Tesla Cat Litter Box. The litter box keeps the same polygon count and wraps its tray in an enclosed, dome-like housing. The plain version is Royalty Free, while the branded variant carries Editorial Uses Only and suits product reviews or tech news. Available since 2023, both pieces fit lifestyle animation, pet store visuals and smart home interiors beside a sofa.

A big set of Second World War aircraft that fills hangars, runways and museum halls with period planes in one purchase. Fighters, bombers and transports from several air forces appear side by side, giving airfield scenes real variety in silhouette. Propellers, canopies and landing gear stand out as distinct parts, so close shots of a parked plane still hold up.

Every aircraft in the bundle passed CheckMate Pro inspection for clean geometry and orderly part naming. Overlapping UVs let symmetrical wings and tail surfaces share texture space, which keeps the material setup compact. Consistent scale between the models means a small fighter and a heavy bomber can park on one apron believably.

Released in 2018 at $1199, the collection costs far less than commissioning this many period aircraft from scratch. History channels, educational books, strategy games and aviation museum displays all draw on planes like these. Olive drab, bare silver and black and white invasion stripes are the paint schemes audiences expect from the era.

USS Cowpens CG-63 is a Ticonderoga-class guided missile cruiser, rebuilt here in heavy detail for close naval shots. A budget of 1,382,544 polygons and 1,533,351 vertices covers radar arrays, missile cells, gun mounts and crowded masts. The angular deckhouse and its flat radar faces give the ship the boxy profile that marks this class at sea.

CheckMate Pro certification confirms clean topology and clearly named parts, so turrets and antennas are easy to select. Non-overlapping UVs keep every hull plate unique, which helps when adding rust streaks, waterline grime or fresh haze gray paint. Black boot topping and white hull numbers stand out against the gray, especially in low morning light. At this density the model holds up in tight shots of the bridge, where windows and railings fill the frame.

Available since 2016 at $289, the cruiser serves naval simulations, history programs and military strategy games. A tracking shot along the bow wave as the warship gains speed shows off the hull detail best.

This domestic rooster struts in a looping walk set up for Blender, ready to cross barnyards, village lanes and cartoon farms. Its 20,913 polygons and 29,569 vertices shape the red comb, the fleshy lobes under the beak and the long arched tail. Each step lifts the scaly feet high while the head pumps forward, the motion people associate with a proud bird.

Built to CheckMate specification, the mesh has clean topology that deforms smoothly through the stride. Non-overlapping UVs keep the golden neck hackles, dark body plumage and bright face on separate texture areas. Tail and neck feathers are layered shapes, so they catch light in tiers instead of reading as one block.

The bird arrived in 2026 at $249 and opens natively in Blender with its walk stored in a single file. Farm games, children's cartoons and agriculture explainers are the usual places for a strutting rooster like this. Offset the timing on a few instances and the courtyard looks lively without hand-animating each bird.

Several Russian military submarine designs come together in this rigged collection, ready for naval documentaries and underwater strategy scenes. Grouping the boats lets a shot compare hull shapes or build a flotilla instead of showing one lonely vessel. Long dark hulls carry tall sails with dive planes, and the sterns end in shrouded propellers or large screws.

Controls move rudders, hydroplanes and propellers on every CheckMate Pro approved boat, so each submarine can dive, turn or surface during an animation. Non-overlapping UVs leave room for hull rust, anechoic tile patterns and faded numbers without texture conflicts.

Available since 2018 at $249, the collection suits naval history programs, military games and defense explainers. Underwater fog and caustic light turn the black hulls into ominous silhouettes in deep sequences. Moored at an icy pier with deck lights glowing, the boats also fit cold northern base scenes. Analysts can line the hulls up by size to explain how attack boats differ from missile carriers.
